text: Immigration does not solve population decline.

quoted_tweet.author: Jesús Fernández-Villaverde
quoted_tweet.text:
¿Cómo sería la población de España en un mundo en el que la inmigración neta a España desde 1995 a 2026 hubiera sido cero en vez de la observada?

Para calcular este escenario, tomo la estructura de población de 1995 y asumo que la fecundidad y mortalidad por edad hubieran sido las mismas que hemos observado. Esta hipótesis no es necesariamente realista, pero sí me parece que nos da unos resultados sobre los que podemos empezar a pensar.

Cada lector puede, mentalmente, ajustar la fecundidad hacia arriba (por ejemplo, con menos inmigración el precio de la vivienda sería más bajo con casi total probabilidad) o hacia abajo (ciertos grupos de inmigrantes tienen fecundidad más alta que la media). 

Particularmente, no creo que haga mucha diferencia en la práctica lo que uno asuma sobre la fecundidad: unos cientos de miles de personas en una dirección o la otra a lo sumo.

No hace falta ajustar la mortalidad: calculo tasas por edad y no creo que estas fueran diferentes en mi escenario.

Lo que más me sorprende es que la inmigración ha generado una subida de la población con respecto al escenario base de 11,1 millones (los inmigrantes y sus hijos nacidos en España), pero el porcentaje de población de 15 a 64 años apenas ha cambiado: tenemos un 66,3% en ese tramo frente al 64,2% en el escenario base.

Y ese cambio de 64,2% a 66,3% no solo no resuelve nada, sino que empeora las cosas. Dado que tenemos un Estado del bienestar altamente redistributivo y la mayoría de la inmigración ha sido de baja cualificación (que son personas con valor presente descontado negativo para el presupuesto público, sí, también en equilibrio general), casi seguro que hemos empeorado la sostenibilidad de las cuentas públicas en el largo plazo.

Hemos cambiado España de manera muy profunda y  lo hemos hecho sin pensar mucho en las consecuencias.

quoted_tweet.author: 宝玉
quoted_tweet.text:
REA：让 AI 智能体帮你逆向没有源码的软件

开源项目 REA（Reverse Engineer Anything）把逆向分析工具接到了 Claude Code、Codex、Cursor 这类 AI 编程智能体上。看到别人 App 里有个好功能，可以让智能体去拆这个程序，讲清楚功能是怎么实现的，附上证据，再在你自己的项目里写一个类似的。逆向分析指的是手里没有源代码，从编译好的程序反推它是怎么写的。

REA 本身是一个 MCP 服务。MCP 是 AI 智能体调用外部工具的通用接口，接上以后，智能体在对话里就能直接调用 REA 的分析功能。安装只需一行命令 npx rea-agents setup，它会注册到 Claude Code、Codex、Cursor、Gemini CLI、Grok Build 等智能体里，改配置前会先备份并让你确认。不用智能体的话，也可以在终端里直接跑命令。

能分析的东西很多。原生程序（直接编译成机器码的软件）要借助 Hopper、Ghidra 或 IDA 这几款反汇编工具，把机器码还原成汇编和近似 C 语言的伪代码。Electron 应用（用网页技术做的桌面软件，比如 Notion）可以直接拆开安装包里的 ASAR 归档文件，理清模块和进程间通信，不需要额外工具。此外还支持 .NET 程序、安卓 APK、固件、网站、抓包记录、以太坊合约字节码，以及在 Linux 和 macOS 上记录程序运行时的行为。

分析在本机进行，REA 不上传目标程序，但分析结果会交给智能体背后的模型服务商，数据怎么处理看各家政策。

项目给了三个案例。一是经典打砖块游戏 DX-Ball：从一次播放音效的调用，追到根据球的位置计算左右声道的函数，把不完整的伪代码还原成 C 代码，3205 组测试结果和原版一致，编译出的 63 个字节也和原版完全相同。二是 Notion 桌面版：追踪复制粘贴从界面一路经过预加载脚本、进程间通信到主进程的完整链路。三是日本老电脑 PC-98 上的游戏《东方幻想乡》（TH04）：从 16 位指令里还原出弹幕子弹环的角度算法。

对安全研究员、做老游戏复刻和软件保存的人来说，以前要自己对着反汇编工具一行行读、一层层追调用，现在可以让智能体先追，人来核对它给出的证据。普通开发者想研究竞品某个功能的做法，也多了一条路。

README 显示项目在 GitHub 上已有 5 万星。npm 包今年 7 月首次发布，最新的 6.3.0 版今天刚发。

使用前注意两点。项目声明只支持合法的逆向研究，授权和合规由使用者自己负责，逆向别人的软件可能违反用户协议或版权法规。项目还说明从未发行或背书任何加密货币，借用 REA 名字的代币都与它无关。

https://github.com/morluto/rea

Figma's Dylan Field on why design is the new code, and where the value goes as models get better:

"If you believe that coding models will continue to get better, then you also believe that it's more outer loop architecture, the decisions you make about how to go build a system that matter, not the code itself."

"The code is material, and then the value rises to the top and that becomes brand, it becomes product design, your marketing, your point of view in the world, and I think overall your judgment calls and strategy."

"Product design is really at the center of a lot of that."

"For designers, they will have a bigger role to play if they step up. Not everyone will step up. Some people will be like, 'But I liked what I was doing.'"

 "Overall the way you'll shape products is through design."

@zoink w/ @sophiadew on @MTSLive

Airbnb's Brian Chesky on the classic management philosophy, and why he rejects it:

"Go through the list of great CEOs, almost none of them that I'm aware of do recurring one-on-ones... Jensen Huang does not do recurring one-on-ones, famously."

"I do think a CEO should meet one-on-one with your people. I don't think it should be recurring... If you wanna get time with me, get a meeting with me. If you wanna call me, call me. Bump into me, talk to me. But most of my recurring meetings are group meetings."

"If there's lots of one-way kinda sensitive topics, there's probably something wrong in the company... If we're having all these sensitive conversations, well, why are they so sensitive? Why can't other people hear about them?"

"If I have a one-on-one with you and you tell me there's a problem and we debate it and we say, 'Here's the solution,' we haven't consulted anyone else. So now we just made a decision and no one else helped, consulted, or knew how we made that decision."

"'Hire great people, trust them, let them do their job, stay out of the details, do recurring one-on-ones.' I don't believe any of that, and I wanna acknowledge that many great leaders do."

@bchesky w/ @sampjacobs

Dmitri Dolgov of @Waymo on how to tell if you’re one year away from shipping or ten:

"One pattern that I've seen over and over again is do you have convergence of discovery? The problems that you are seeing today, how different are they from the problems you saw six months ago?"

"As you're pushing on the system, does it feel like you have stability, and you're just iteratively improving your metrics in the same areas?"

"Or does it feel like every six months the landscape is shifting from under you and the problems of today are very different from what you saw a while ago?

"If you don't have that stability, then that's often a good indicator that you got some ways to go."

"If you think you're six months or a year away from deployment, do you have a scorecard that if it were green today would allow you to deploy with confidence?"

"If you don't have one, you're saving that for later, often that turns out to be more difficult than you expected, and there's a long distance to go."

"But if you already have one and you're seeing stability in your discovery and stability in your metrics, and it's just a matter of closing the gap, that is a really good indicator that you're getting pretty close."

@dmitri_dolgov w/ South Park Commons

.@heronpower CEO Drew Baglino on the 40-year streak that kept US electricity flat while the economy grew, and why it just ended:

"We benefited from energy efficiency from the '70s... until like the 2010s. You saw efficiency everywhere... And all of that energy efficiency more or less negated the growth in energy services."

"The energy services were growing over time in the United States, but the net electricity delivered to accomplish those energy services stayed basically flat. And the same thing even happened in data centers."

"If you look at the efficiency of compute, even with all the AI things that are going on, in terms of flops per watt, it's really gone up an immense amount from the first data centers to today."

"And that has allowed more and more compute capability for the same percentage of GDP electricity production."

"Now it's changing... We are seeing electricity growth higher than it's ever been before. And that's not just because the benefits of energy efficiency are tailing off, it's because we are seeing broad based demand for more electricity: compute, transportation, industrial electrification."

"Electricity as a carrier is incredibly flexible... whether it's for intelligence or for heating, I see it as a great thing and wanna accelerate it."

@baglino @heronpower
